speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, it introduces new measures to the disciplinary framework for lawyers to supplement the existing suite of measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It also contains certain miscellaneous and technical amendments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The majority of the amendments being introduced in this Bill are at the request of the Law Society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The legal profession is a noble one and members of the profession must continue to hold themselves to the highest ethical standards of professional conduct.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is essential to Singapore's reputation as an international legal services hub as well as for the protection of the public and clients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Under the current disciplinary framework for lawyers, the range of disciplinary measures available to the Law Society Council include issuing a warning or reprimand to the lawyer, and/or ordering the lawyer to pay a penalty.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In more egregious and serious cases of misconduct, the Court of three Judges can order that a lawyer be suspended or struck off the roll of advocates and solicitors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This Bill introduces more nuanced and calibrated options to the range of disciplinary measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The amendments seek to deal with the root causes of certain types of misconduct, reduce recidivism, as well as widen the range of measures available to deal with less serious disciplinary matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clauses 2, 22, 23, 24 and 26 to 29 of the Bill thus expand the range of measures that may be imposed during disciplinary proceedings to include remedial measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Such remedial measures can be imposed in addition to, or in lieu of, the current options which are available to the Law Society Council.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The amendments will enable the Council to prescribe remedial measures, such as those which involve training, counselling and other means of rehabilitation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This does not mean that serious cases of misconduct will be dealt with lightly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Rather, it strengthens our disciplinary framework for lawyers with a broader range of disciplinary options that can be imposed, together with other existing measures, or in lieu of, where appropriate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The second main set of amendments introduced a framework to deal with unclaimed client money and unclaimed intervention money.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Client money refers to the money which lawyers and law practices may receive in the course of client engagements, to hold on behalf of their clients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Act currently requires all client money to be held and administered by the practising lawyer in a client account.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The money remains in the client account until it is paid out based on the client's instructions or returned to the client.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, the Act does not currently specify what happens when client money is left unclaimed in a client account, for example, if the client becomes uncontactable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In these cases, the lawyers and law practices concerned would be unable to close the client account, and must hold the unclaimed client money indefinitely, incurring costs in administering the client accounts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Lawyers who want to retire and dissolve their law practices, but who are holding onto unclaimed client moneys, are in a difficult position.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: They either have to find another practising lawyer willing to take over the administration of the client account, or they would be unable to retire and must continue to bear the expenses of maintaining their law practices and these client accounts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 18 of the Bill provides a practical solution to this problem.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Solicitors and Singapore law practices will be able to transfer unclaimed client money into the UM Fund, provided that they satisfy certain requirements and the Law Society approves the transfer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These requirements will be prescribed by the Law Society Council with the Minister's approval and will include what reasonable efforts the solicitor or Singapore law practice should have made to return the money, before the Society will approve a transfer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Such "reasonable efforts" will take various circumstances into account, for example, more robust steps may be required in the case of larger amounts, and account may be taken of practical issues which may arise in cases of very old client accounts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Provision is made for the framework to be extended, where appropriate, to foreign lawyers and foreign law practices or entities regulated under the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Once the money is in the UM Fund, should the lawful owner of the unclaimed client money surface after the money has been transferred to the UM Fund, the new section 70L provides a statutory mechanism for such persons to apply to the Law Society for the transferred money to be returned.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Such claimants may also approach their lawyers, and their lawyers can apply to the Law Society on the claimants' behalf for the transferred money to be returned to the claimants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Details of the statutory mechanism will be prescribed in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, the new section 70L(5) states that the Law Society has the power to make discretionary, or ex gratia, payments from the UM Fund to claimants who apply after the time bar.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Law Society's discretion will be exercised on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In exercising its discretion, the Law Society will consider factors, such as the reasons why the claimant did not approach the Law Society before the time bar, for example, whether they were prevented by matters, such as fraud or disability, and whether there will be undue hardship if no ex-gratia payment is made.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Law Society may invest or use the money in the UM Fund, as prescribed, to fund pro bono services provided by the Law Society or by any of its wholly-owned subsidiaries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This allows the unclaimed client money to be applied towards the public good instead of idling in a client account.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It should be noted that the issue of unclaimed client money is not unique to Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Solicitors in England and Wales have a framework under which a solicitor may pay unclaimed client money below a certain threshold to a charity, provided that certain requirements are fulfilled.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I mentioned earlier that unclaimed intervention money will be brought within this framework.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Under the current Act, the Law Society has the power to intervene in a lawyer’s practice in specified circumstances, for example, where a sole proprietor has died.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As part of the intervention, the Law Society may take over the administration of the lawyer’s client accounts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The client money in these client accounts is called intervention money.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It is because the Law Society has intervened.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The intervention money is transferred into a special account held by the Law Society for the Law Society to administer, including returning the intervention money to the lawyer’s clients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Act currently provides that intervention money which has remained unclaimed for six years in the special account will be transferred to the Compensation Fund.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In the event that a claimant surfaces after six years, the Law Society has the discretion to make an ex-gratia payment out of the Compensation Fund.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Similarly, in the event that a claimant surfaces after six years, any ex-gratia payments by the Law Society will be paid out of the UM Fund instead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I now deal with the introduction of a registration category for non-practising foreign law experts to appear in the SICC to make submissions on matters of foreign law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clauses 8 to 16 of the Bill seek to allow a non-practising foreign law expert, such as an academic, to appear in SICC to make submissions on matters of foreign law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will allow experts with specialised knowledge on matters of foreign law, based on their training, study or experience, or who are otherwise qualified, to appear in relevant proceedings in the SICC and relevant appeals in the Court of Appeal to submit on matters of foreign law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Applications for registration of a law expert can be made to the Registrar.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill also extends the current complaints process, which is currently applicable to foreign lawyers registered to appear in SICC, to these foreign law experts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Related amendments to the Supreme Court of Judicature Act are also made.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It is common in international commercial arbitration practice for law experts to make submissions on foreign law before tribunals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Extending this option to users of SICC will further enhance the attractiveness of SICC as a premier international commercial Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, clauses 3 and 20 of the Bill amend the Act to give the Law Society Council the power to require prescribed classes of solicitors who practise or intend to practise in a prescribed area of law, to make a declaration when applying for a practising certificate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This amendment puts into effect the recommendation of the Study Committee on Professional Standards and Etiquette in Court under the auspices of the Singapore Academy of Law’s Professional Affairs Committee.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The test is not intended to be an onerous requirement but will serve as a self-learning and self-assessment tool to remind solicitors of their obligations as members of a noble profession.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will propagate good practices as well as reinforce and serve as a useful reminder of changes relevant to the practice area.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Council also has the powers to exempt a solicitor or a class of solicitors from making a declaration, if the Council is satisfied that the solicitor or the class of solicitors is already equipped with the knowledge and skills required for practice in that area of the law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, currently, the Law Society Council is only able to apply interest, dividends and other accretions of capital arising from the Compensation Fund which consists of contributions from solicitors, to purchase and maintain a library for its members’ use.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Fourth, clause 4 of the Bill extends an exception relating to the requirements for a practising certificate, which are currently applicable to solicitors employed by the Law Society, to those employed by wholly-owned subsidiaries of the Law Society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, only Singapore law practices structured as sole proprietorships and partnerships may form a group law practice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This updates the group law practice scheme which was introduced prior to the introduction of law corporations and limited liability law partnerships.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: And lastly, clauses 5, 6 and 7 of the Bill repeal section 36F of the current Act and makes consequential amendments as this category of registration of lawyers has been subsumed into other legislation categories under the regulatory regime and is no longer needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In summary, all these amendments that I have mentioned will ensure that our framework for the legal industry continues to remain up to date and responsive to changes in the legal landscape.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The legal profession plays an important role − an integral role − in the administration of justice in our rule of law society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Through ways, such as providing legal advice, representation and promoting legal literacy through education, lawyers play an important role in access to justice.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One of these functions could be pro bono services as clause 4 also allows solicitors employed under the wholly-owned subsidiary to apply for a practising certificate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is also supplemented through clause 19 that allows the wholly-owned subsidiary to use accretions to capital from the Compensation Fund.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Through the new section 70J(3)(b), the new UM Fund would also complement that financial support for the Law Society's pro bono services and the activities of a wholly-owned subsidiary.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These amendments would support the ongoing pro bono efforts by the Law Society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At this point in time, I should declare that I am a legal practitioner at the Singapore Bar.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One of the stated missions of the Law Society is to ensure access to justice for all, and one way this has been done is through pro bono services.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some of the excellent work is reflected in the Community Legal Clinic Scheme, the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS) and the Ad Hoc Pro Bono Referral.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Not restricted to individuals, the Law Society also works with voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) and charities which are unable to afford legal consultation and representation due to limited resources.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Law Awareness seeks to "break 'legal jargon'" into accessible "easy-to-understand elements" for the public through talks, exhibits, resource materials.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, these welcome amendments enhance the Law Society’s contributions to our community.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This provides for another option that law practices may choose to organise themselves within, allowing for more flexibility in how practices may choose to position themselves in the legal industry.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill also provides for law experts to appear before SICC and relevant appeals in the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The expertise from which SICC can draw on in a proceeding is no longer limited to practising solicitors, persons admitted under section 15 ad hoc admissions or foreign lawyers registered under section 36P.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But these legal experts serve a separate function.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They come into the picture when the SICC orders that a question of foreign law be determined on the basis of submissions, instead of proof.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thirdly, this Bill seeks to further regulate the Bar.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On this theme, I have two clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My second clarification for the Minister is on the introduction and expansion of remedial measures.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While it may provide for an intermediate option in addressing situations, the Bill sets few parameters on what kind of remedial measures Council can make under the new section 97A.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While Ministerial approval is necessary, it seems as though the power is constrained only by the purpose of the rule, that is, new section 97A paragraph (a) which says "to address any issue concerning the professional practice, etiquette, conduct or discipline of a regulated legal practitioner" and paragraph (b) "any requirements that Council may specify for compliance with an order of the Council under section 88(1A) or 94(3A)".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The latter seems to include warning, reprimand and financial penalty as remedial orders.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My clarification for the good Minister is why are the safeguards in section 88(2) and section 88(3) not extended to the new subsections (1A) and (1B) even though they may carry similar consequences?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In short, my position is that any remedial actions must also be fair to the practitioners, and the process in deciding whether a remedial action should be administered should also be fair to the practitioner.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fourthly, Sir, through the setting up of the UM Fund, clients’ interests continue to be safeguarded, while providing a practical solution for some solicitors’ conundrum.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These changes would allow lawyers who wish to retire to do so, by relieving lawyers of the burden and expense of maintaining the client account.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is especially pertinent as the solution mechanism of "intervention money" being paid into the Compensation Fund does not reflect our current legal industry landscape where law firms may not always continue across generations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, the UM Fund would allow solicitors to avoid this conundrum in the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, these unclaimed monies can be used for a public good.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The purpose under which a solicitor may apply to transfer money into the UM Fund will be restricted under section 70J(2) and (3).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this manner, the UM Fund provides a practical win-win solution for all.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill augments that aim and, therefore, I support it.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Legal Profession (Amendment) Bill introduces various amendments to the Legal Profession Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The introduction of a further disciplinary option that can be imposed against an errant legal practitioner and the creation of the UM Fund are noteworthy innovations that should be welcomed by Members of this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to make three short points on the proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Compensation Fund is a fund administered by the Council of the Law Society to serve a public purpose in that grants may be paid out of the Fund to mitigate loss suffered by any person due to dishonesty of a lawyer or a member of his staff.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A similar amendment was made in 2001 for penalties paid as a result of disciplinary proceedings to be paid to the Society, instead of the Consolidated Fund, so that the Law Society could use the monies for worthy causes, such as providing pro bono services or creating legal awareness.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What would be the consequent effect on the Compensation Fund, in terms of its funding level, if the monies were to be channelled to the Society?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would the Fund have sufficient funds to meet claims from members of the public?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, given that the Law Society has just moved to e-voting recently, what is the expected amount of revenue generated for use by the Society from penalties for failing to vote?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, it does not appear that the proposed amendments require the Law Society to take reasonable efforts to return the monies to the owners.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I note that the hon Senior Minister of State stated that the Law Society requires solicitors to expend reasonable efforts before they are being allowed to transfer those monies to the Law Society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But vis-à-vis the Law Society itself, it is not clear what steps the Law Society would have to undertake and who checks on the Society in relation to the steps the Law Society would have to undertake to locate these claimants or potential claimants.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given the breadth of professional conduct rules legal practitioners are bound by, could the hon Senior Minister of State please clarify what kind of remedial measures are contemplated, and in what situations would remedial measures be imposed?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I believe the hon Member Mr Christopher de Souza made a similar request.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I wonder if there is any reason for the proposed amendments not to provide for the Court of Three Judges, which sits at the apex of the disciplinary process to also impose remedial measures.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would the hon Senior Minister of State accept that the absence of the empowering provision does not curtail the powers of the Court of Three Judges to impose requirements on legal practitioners, such as undertakings to the Court which may mirror obligations imposed through the remedial measures?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications I raised, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lawyers I spoke to welcome, in particular, three changes that have been proposed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The first relates to the appointment of law experts in cases before SICC, a move, no doubt put in place to improve the quality of arguments raised in SICC on foreign law issues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The second relates to the establishment of the UM Fund to be administered by the Law Society of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The amendment will result in certain monies that are unclaimed being put to use in, amongst other things, pro bono services.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Previously, the options were limited to the issuance of a warning, a reprimand or the imposition of a fine.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These were aimed at censuring and punishing the errant regulated legal practitioner and may not have addressed root causes for the impeached conduct.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While the precise type of remedial measures that may be imposed will be set out in further subsidiary legislation, it is heartening to see that there is now another option available which is not entirely punitive in nature.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, it is with this last change that I now seek clarifications.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill proposes to allow an Inquiry Committee to recommend to the Council of the Law Society of Singapore that a penalty, warning, reprimand, and/or requirement of compliance with remedial measures be imposed on a practitioner, without any formal investigation by a Disciplinary Tribunal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Council of the Law Society can then make such a determination under the new section 87 of the Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lawyers I have spoken to are concerned about the mandatory imposition because this seems to render the practitioner's opportunity to be heard on the matter under section 88(3) futile.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the interest of fairness and in line with the right to be heard, the practitioner really ought to be able to make her or his case on the matter and section 88(3) should remain.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, I note that the imposition of the remedial measures by Council is sought to be introduced by way of a new section 88(1A), but section 88(3) of the Act remains unchanged.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This seems to suggest that a practitioner will not be heard before remedial measures are imposed upon him or her by the Council.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I declare that I am a lawyer in private practice.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Legal Profession Act and the various subsidiary legislation, including the Legal Profession (Professional Conduct) Rules and the Legal Profession (Solicitor's Account) Rules, govern the profession and help ensure that the integrity of the profession is preserved.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am heartened, therefore, by the further enhancements that I believe will ensure that the high standards expected of the profession will be maintained.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I wish to record my observations on several proposed amendments in this Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is a laudable move in that it allows for a suite of more nuanced, meaningful and fair sanctions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The profession calls for high standards of conduct, and I believe we should continue to assert this.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, it is important to have regulation that seeks to encourage good behaviour and rehabilitate undesirable conduct, instead of being merely punitive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I, therefore, hope that in its application, the directions or orders for remedial measures will help to encourage better conduct amongst the lawyers who face disciplinary proceedings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For far too long, lawyers have had difficulties in dealing with monies put in as deposit by clients or deposited in favour of the clients, who subsequently cannot be reached.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Lawyers are required to keep monies belonging to clients in the client's account, until there is a proper invoice or proper instructions are given for monies to be paid out.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: When the clients cannot be contacted, the lawyer then has difficulties.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There have been situations where the lawyer cannot close the firm because of this outstanding issue.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Typically, the lawyer would ask another lawyer to take over the account, but this can be a hassle.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I appreciate that the proposed clause 70L allows for a channel for the client or claimant to apply to the Law Society for payment of the whole or part of the unclaimed money and, upon payment, the Law Society and lawyer are discharged from liability to the claimant for the amount paid.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am heartened that there is provision in the proposed section 70L(5) to deal with situations where claims come in after the expiry of the six-year period.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe this reflects reasonableness and compassion, values which should be upheld by the fraternity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The provision of pro bono services, in my view, is a key component within the community as it helps to augment the existing Legal Aid scheme that is available.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I hope that with the access to this new Fund, there would be more resources and additional effort to bridge any gaps in the provision of legal services, especially to those who may not meet the criteria to obtain Legal Aid.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As mentioned above, I believe that the proposed amendments will ensure that the high standards expected of this profession will be maintained.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Christopher de Souza inquired about the circumstances under which remedial measures may be imposed on a lawyer and what kind of remedial measures can be imposed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These provide for a more nuanced, tailored and effective means to address the root causes of certain types of misconduct as well as reduce recidivism.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Such remedial measures will be set out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai also asked why the proposed amendments do not provide for the Court of three Judges to impose remedial measures, unlike the Law Society Council or the Disciplinary Tribunal.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The answer is that the system design is such that by the time it comes before the Court of three Judges, it means the case has gone well beyond remedial measures.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Court of three Judges is disciplinary in nature, not remedial.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: By the time a complaint involving misconduct by a lawyer comes before the Court of three Judges, three stages in the disciplinary review process would have been completed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, a Review Committee would have decided that the complaint is of such substance that it must be referred to an Inquiry Committee.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, the Inquiry Committee would already have found that the case of misconduct has been made out against the lawyer, and it would have taken the view that the complaint must be referred to a Disciplinary Tribunal.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Third, the Disciplinary Tribunal would have determined that cause of sufficient gravity for disciplinary action exists such that the matter has to be referred to the Court of three Judges.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As Members will see, it is a vigorous process and one in which less serious infractions capable of remediation are weeded out early and dealt with.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Each step of the process deals with increasing levels of severity of lapses or infractions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The complaints which come before the Court of three Judges are, therefore, the ones that involve egregious cases of misconduct for which the remedial actions are not sufficient or appropriate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But that said, as pointed out by Mr Murali Pillai, that does not foreclose the Court of three Judges from imposing requirements on legal practitioners, such as undertakings to the Court which may mirror obligations imposed through remedial measures.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We do not condone bad behaviour by lawyers and we wish to send a message that errant lawyers will not be let off lightly for serious cases of misconduct.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This brings me to Mr Louis Ng and Mr Christopher de Souza's point on the correlation between the amendments to section 88(1) read with section 88(3) and the opportunity to be heard under the latter provision.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As mentioned, the disciplinary process for lawyers is multi-tiered.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A lawyer who is the subject of a complaint may have reasonable opportunity to be heard by the Inquiry Committee.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: After the Council has considered the report of the Inquiry Committee, it can determine that no formal investigation is required and no penalty will be imposed on the lawyer.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Council can also determine that there should be a formal investigation by the Disciplinary Tribunal.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What section 88 deals with is the intermediate situation where it has been determined by the Council that some wrongdoing has occurred but no formal investigation is needed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it does not need to be referred to the Disciplinary Tribunal.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With the amendments, this now allows for two options under section 88.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, the existing option for imposing a warning, reprimand or penalty continues to apply.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These sanctions are entered as adverse orders against the lawyers named on the roll.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, the new remedial measures, which are rehabilitative in nature, can also be considered.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As mentioned, these remedial measures may include counselling and training for the lawyer.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the event Council wishes to impose the former – meaning the reprimand or the penalty – the lawyer is always offered an opportunity to be heard.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If having heard his explanations, Council remains of the view that those sanctions continue to be appropriate, those sanctions will be applied.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is how it is currently done and, therefore, there is no substantive change to the operations of section 88(1).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Where the lawyer has been heard by Council and Council agrees that a warning, reprimand or penalty is not appropriate, Council may, pursuant to the new section 88(1A), impose a remedial measure that does not go into the lawyer's disciplinary records.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And in that situation, he would already have been heard in the first instance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, this addresses both of Mr Louis Ng's points as well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked whether there are sufficient monies in the Compensation Fund.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Compensation Fund was first established in 1962 and it is maintained and administered by the Law Society.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Where it has been proven to the satisfaction of Council that a person has sustained loss as a result of dishonesty by a lawyer, the Law Society may, if the Council thinks fit, make a grant to that person out of the Compensation Fund with the purpose of relieving or mitigating that loss.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As such, there are sufficient monies in the Compensation Fund to meet the purposes of the Fund.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Currently, where Members fail to vote at Council elections, they pay a penalty of S$500, which is credited to the Compensation Fund.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, the Law Society's position is that the failure to vote at Council elections has no nexus with professional misconduct but rather pertains to the administration of the Law Society or its governance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As such, penalty sums should be credited to the Law Society instead of the Compensation Fund.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will allow the Law Society to use the monies in a manner that advances the public interest.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, as the Member has highlighted, allowing the penalty sum to be credited to the Law Society also aligns with the current crediting of penalties to the Law Society under section 95 of the Act, where the Council has ordered a lawyer to pay a penalty.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about the expected amount of monies generated from penalties for failing to vote, given that the Law Society has moved to electronic voting for its Council elections recently.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The average penalty collected prior to the implementation of online voting was about S$28,000.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Since the implementation of online voting in October 2016, the amount of penalty sums collected has decreased significantly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For the period April 2017 to January 2018, the penalty sums collected decreased to S$13,500.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hence, the amount in question is not large.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about the operation and thinking behind clause 20 of the Bill, which relates to the requirement for prescribed classes of solicitors who practise or intend to practise in a prescribed area of law, to make a declaration when applying for a practising certificate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As mentioned, this amendment puts into effect the recommendation of the Study Committee on Professional Standards and Etiquette in Court under the auspices of the Singapore Academy of Law's Professional Affairs Committee, which looked into issues of professional standards and Court etiquette for the Bar.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One of the Study Committee's recommendations was for the Law Society to introduce an online test to remind members of their professional obligations as counsel, and decorum and etiquette in Court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Law Society's intention is to prescribe that solicitors who practise in the area of litigation will need to complete a short online test and declare that they have done the test before applying for or renewing their practising certificates.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This online test will be a self-assessment and self-learning tool to propagate good practices, as well as to reinforce and serve as a useful reminder of changes which are relevant to their practice area.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For new entrants to the profession, and for those for whom litigation may not be a core practice area, they will benefit from having more guidance by way of this online test.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The amendments in the Bill also allow the Law Society Council to exempt a solicitor or a class of solicitors if it is satisfied that the solicitor or class of solicitors is already equipped with the knowledge and skills required for practice in that area of the law.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, I will deal with the UM Fund.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked why the proposed amendments do not require the Law Society to take reasonable efforts to return the money to the owners.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The reason is because, that should have been done by the solicitors as part and parcel of their duties even before they pay the money over to the UM Fund.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Law Society's role is primarily that of a repository of the unclaimed moneys and administration of the approved uses to which it can be put.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Its other role is to make discretionary decisions on payments out to clients after expiration of the limitation period.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Broadly summarising, the new section 70K provides that a solicitor or Singapore law practice may apply to pay into the UM Fund, money which should be paid to the client but which they are unable to do so, despite making such reasonable efforts as the Law Society may require.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in other words, the lawyer or the law firm has to make all reasonable efforts first, before they can pay money over to the Fund.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As to what the "reasonable efforts" are, the subsidiary legislation will prescribe what the required "reasonable efforts" are, taking into account relevant circumstances previously mentioned.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In turn, the Law Society may not approve a transfer unless it is satisfied that the prescribed “reasonable efforts” requirements have been satisfied.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The burden of taking steps to return the money is rightly placed on the lawyers because they are the ones with the primary duty to return the money to the client, and they are the ones who have the files and records and will, therefore, be in a better position to contact the clients.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It would not be practical to expect the Law Society to make efforts to search for the owners of the money when their own lawyers have been unable to find them despite reasonable efforts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In any case, as I mentioned earlier, if the lawful owner of the money surfaces after the money has been transferred, they will still be able to apply to the Law Society for the transferred money to be returned to them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This strikes a balance on what is fair on the lawyer, the client and the Law Society.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If implemented, such a duty may reduce the number of new cases of unclaimed client money being accumulated.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The subsidiary legislation will also prescribe in greater detail how the money in the Fund may be used and, in this regard, the Minister must also approve any subsidiary legislation which the Law Society Council makes for the purposes of the framework.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Thus, it would be fair to say that the people who will benefit from the new UM Fund will be members of the public who are in need of, and eligible for, the Law Society's pro bono services.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Separately, Ms Rahayu Mahzam had inquired about the intent of the new section 70K(4).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The intent of the provision is to set a limitation period of six years against all actions that may be brought against any lawyer or law practice who has ever held the unclaimed client money previously.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The provision distinguishes between (a) the lawyer who transferred the unclaimed client money into the UM Fund, and (b) any lawyer who may have held the money previously, to account for the possibility that some unclaimed client money may have been passed from one retiring lawyer to another practising lawyer previously.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Such retired lawyers will, therefore, also have the clarity and certainty arising from the limitation period, too.
